nameStory: The Conifer Mazegill gets its name from the intricate maze-like pattern of its pores and gills on the underside, which resembles a tiny labyrinth. It's called a 'conifer' specialist because it almost exclusively feeds on softwood trees like pine, spruce, and fir. The scientific name 'sepiarium' refers to its brownish coloration, like old sepia photographs.
description: The Conifer Mazegill is a bracket fungus that forms tough, leathery shelves jutting out from dead conifer wood. These brownish, semi-circular brackets typically measure 2-6 inches across and have a distinctive rusty-brown color that darkens with age. Unlike many bracket fungi with simple pores, this species has a unique maze-like pattern on its underside that combines elongated pores with gill-like ridges. It's a wood-rotting fungus that causes brown rot, breaking down the cellulose in dead coniferous trees.

idTips.label: Pores/Gills
idTips.description: The underside shows a distinctive maze-like pattern of elongated pores mixed with gill-like ridges that run radially from where it attaches to wood. This labyrinthine structure is rusty-brown to yellow-brown in color.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Forms tough, leathery brackets that are semicircular to fan-shaped, with a velvety to slightly fuzzy upper surface that's brown to rusty-brown, often with darker zones.

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found on dead coniferous wood - pine, spruce, fir, or hemlock logs, stumps, and construction lumber. Rarely if ever on hardwoods.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels tough and leathery when fresh, becoming hard and woody when dry. The surface has a velvety texture that may feel slightly fuzzy to the touch.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces a white to pale yellow spore print, though this is difficult to obtain from bracket fungi.

idTips.label: Safety
idTips.description: This is a woody bracket fungus that's far too tough to be edible. Never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification.

habitat: Look for Conifer Mazegill on dead coniferous trees throughout New England's forests, especially in areas with pine, spruce, fir, and hemlock. It's commonly found on fallen logs, dead standing trees, stumps, and even untreated coniferous lumber in construction. You'll spot it from sea level up to mountain elevations wherever conifers grow.

seasonality.spring: Existing brackets continue growing after winter, often appearing fresher and more colorful as moisture returns. New brackets may begin forming on recently dead wood.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when fresh brackets develop their most vibrant rusty-brown colors. Hot, dry periods may cause brackets to become dormant until moisture returns.
seasonality.fall: Continued growth and spore production, with brackets often reaching their largest size. Fall rains trigger active growth after summer dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Brackets persist year-round as tough, woody structures. Growth slows dramatically, but they remain visible and identifiable even under snow.

funFact: This fungus can literally eat your house - it's one of the most destructive wood decay fungi for coniferous construction lumber, capable of breaking down structural timbers so thoroughly that buildings can collapse, which is why it's sometimes called the 'dry rot fungus' in construction contexts.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other bracket fungi on conifers, but the distinctive maze-like pore pattern is diagnostic - other brackets have simple round pores or true gills, not this labyrinthine combination. Remember: 'maze pattern = mazegill.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'rusty gilled polypore' in some guides, it's not a true polypore (which have simple pores) or a gilled mushroom - it represents a unique evolutionary solution combining both pore and gill-like structures for spore dispersal.
compareHints: Since this is the only Gloeophyllum species commonly found in New England, compare it to other conifer-loving bracket fungi like the Red Belt Polypore, which has simple round pores and a white margin, or Tinder Polypore, which is much larger and has simple pores. The maze-like pore pattern immediately distinguishes Conifer Mazegill from all other bracket fungi in the region.
